questions.question: How does a HashMap work internally in Java?
questions.title: HashMap Internal Working Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **HashMap uses an array of buckets.** The key's `hashCode()` is used to compute a bucket index. If multiple keys hash to the same bucket (collision), they're stored in a linked list (or tree in Java 8+). Average O(1) get/put; worst case O(n) with all keys in one bucket.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand what's happening under the hood — every Java interview asks this
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying HashMap is always O(1) without mentioning collision and worst case, or not knowing about Java 8's tree bucket optimization
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Java 8 improvement: when a bucket's linked list exceeds 8 entries, it converts to a TreeNode (Red-Black Tree) for O(log n) worst case

sections.title: Hash Table: Array + Linked List (+ Tree in Java 8)
sections.content: A HashMap internally maintains an **array of Node[] buckets** (default capacity 16). For `put(key, value)`: compute `hashCode(key)`, then `index = hash % capacity`. Store the key-value pair at that bucket. For **collision** (two keys same index): Java uses a linked list of nodes at that bucket (chaining). In **Java 8+**: when a bucket's chain exceeds 8 entries and the table size ≥ 64, it converts to a **Red-Black Tree** — improving worst-case from O(n) to **O(log n)**.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Internal structure: array of Node[] (buckets)
- Hash → index calculation: (n-1) & hash (bitwise AND for power-of-2 capacity)
- Collision resolution: chaining (linked list per bucket)
- Java 8: bucket converts to Red-Black Tree when chain length > 8
- Load factor: default 0.75 — rehash when 75% full
- Rehashing: double capacity, recompute all bucket indices — O(n) amortized
- O(1) average for get/put/remove; O(log n) worst case (Java 8+)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: HashMap internally uses an array of buckets. When you call put, it computes the key's hashCode and uses it to find the bucket index. If two keys land in the same bucket, that's a collision — they're stored as a linked list at that bucket. In Java 8, once a bucket's chain exceeds 8 entries, it converts to a Red-Black Tree for O(log n) worst-case instead of O(n). The load factor defaults to 0.75, meaning when 75% of buckets are filled, the map doubles its capacity and rehashes all entries. Average-case operations are O(1) because a good hash function distributes keys evenly.

questions.question: How do you use a HashMap to solve the frequency counting pattern?
questions.title: Frequency Counting with HashMap Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Build a frequency map: iterate the array, using `map.getOrDefault(key, 0) + 1` to count occurrences.** Then query the map in O(1). This pattern solves anagram detection, finding most frequent element, top-k frequency problems — all in O(n) time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical HashMap usage — this pattern appears in 30%+ of array/string interview problems
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a nested loop to count each element instead of a single HashMap pass
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the `getOrDefault` idiom cleanly, and mention `merge()` as the modern Java 8 alternative

sections.title: O(n) Frequency Map Pattern
sections.content: **Build phase**: `map.put(key, map.getOrDefault(key, 0) + 1)` — one pass, O(n). **Query phase**: `map.get(key)` — O(1). **Java 8 cleaner form**: `map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum)` — adds 1 if key exists, puts 1 if it doesn't. This one pattern underlies: anagram check (compare two frequency maps), most frequent element (find max value), top-k elements (use PriorityQueue on the map entries), grouping anagrams (sort key as map key).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- map.getOrDefault(key, 0) + 1: safe increment
- map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum): Java 8 idiomatic form
- map.getOrDefault(key, 0): safe retrieval with fallback
- Build: O(n) time; query: O(1)
- Anagram: two frequency maps equal?
- Most frequent: iterate map.entrySet(), track max value
- Top-k: use PriorityQueue<Map.Entry> sorted by value
- Works for characters, strings, integers

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The frequency counting pattern is one of the most useful HashMap applications. I iterate through the input once, using getOrDefault to safely increment the count for each element — if the key doesn't exist yet it defaults to zero, then I add one. After building the map, I can answer frequency queries in O(1). In Java 8 I'd use map.merge of key, 1, Integer colon colon sum, which is more concise. This single pattern solves anagram detection, finding duplicates, most frequent element, and is the foundation for top-k problems using a PriorityQueue on the map entries.

questions.question: What is the difference between HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap in Java?
questions.title: HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **HashMap**: unordered, O(1) average. **LinkedHashMap**: insertion-order or access-order maintained, O(1) average. **TreeMap**: sorted by key, O(log n) operations. Choose based on whether you need ordering.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the Java collections hierarchy and can choose the right map for the right job
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that LinkedHashMap is used to implement LRU cache, or not knowing that TreeMap is a Red-Black Tree
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the LRU cache use case for LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true, and connect TreeMap to the BST/Red-Black Tree discussion

sections.title: Three Maps, Three Ordering Guarantees
sections.content: **HashMap**: backed by hash table, no ordering guarantee, O(1) average. **LinkedHashMap**: adds a doubly linked list to maintain **insertion order** (or access order if `accessOrder=true` in constructor) — O(1) average, slightly more memory. `accessOrder=true` makes it perfect for **LRU cache**. **TreeMap**: backed by Red-Black Tree, keys in **natural sorted order**, O(log n) for all operations. Useful when you need `firstKey()`, `lastKey()`, `subMap()`, `floorKey()`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- HashMap: O(1), no order — most common choice
- LinkedHashMap: O(1), preserves insertion order
- LinkedHashMap(capacity, loadFactor, true): access order → LRU cache
- TreeMap: O(log n), sorted by key, implements NavigableMap
- TreeMap unique methods: firstKey(), lastKey(), floorKey(), ceilingKey(), subMap()
- All three: O(n) space
- Null keys: HashMap allows one; TreeMap does not (comparison needed)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The three main Map implementations differ in ordering. HashMap gives no ordering guarantee but O(1) operations — it's my default choice. LinkedHashMap maintains insertion order, which is useful when iteration order matters, and with access-order mode it's the standard way to implement an LRU cache. TreeMap keeps keys in sorted natural order using a Red-Black Tree, giving O(log n) operations but enabling range queries like floorKey or subMap. I'd use TreeMap when I need sorted keys or range lookups, LinkedHashMap when order matters, and HashMap for everything else.

questions.question: What is the hashCode and equals contract in Java and why does it matter for HashMap?
questions.title: hashCode equals Contract Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **If two objects are equal (equals() returns true), they must have the same hashCode.** Violating this contract breaks HashMap/HashSet — equal objects would land in different buckets and not be found. Both methods must be overridden together.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core Java OOP — this is a frequent senior/mid question but freshers at product companies face it too
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Overriding equals without overriding hashCode — leads to broken HashMap behavior
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete bug example: two 'equal' Person objects with same name/id would go to different HashMap buckets if hashCode not overridden

sections.title: The Two-Method Contract
sections.content: The contract: (1) If `a.equals(b)` is true, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` **must** be true. (2) If two objects have the same hashCode, they may or may not be equal (collision is OK). **Why it matters for HashMap**: HashMap first uses hashCode to find the bucket, then uses equals to find the exact key within that bucket. If you override equals but not hashCode, two 'equal' objects get different hashCodes → land in different buckets → HashMap can't find them.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Rule: equals true → same hashCode (mandatory)
- Rule: same hashCode → equals may be true or false (OK)
- Override BOTH equals AND hashCode together — always
- IDE/Lombok/@EqualsAndHashCode generate both
- Default Object.hashCode() uses memory address — wrong for value equality
- HashSet also relies on this contract for uniqueness checks
- Breaking the contract → bugs that are hard to reproduce (depend on JVM run)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The hashCode and equals contract states that if two objects are equal according to equals, they must have the same hashCode. This is crucial for HashMap because it uses hashCode to find the bucket and then equals to find the exact key. If I override equals for value comparison but forget to override hashCode, two logically equal objects get different hash codes, land in different buckets, and the HashMap can't find them — leading to subtle bugs like a key you just put not being found on get. In practice I always override both together, using IDE generation or Lombok's EqualsAndHashCode annotation.

questions.question: How would you use a HashMap to find the longest subarray with sum equal to k?
questions.title: Longest Subarray Sum K HashMap | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use prefix sums stored in a HashMap.** For each index, compute the running sum. If `sum - k` exists in the map, a subarray ending at the current index has sum k. Store the first occurrence of each prefix sum to maximize subarray length. O(n) time, O(n) space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Advanced HashMap usage — prefix sum + HashMap is a classic O(n) pattern for subarray problems
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a brute-force O(n²) or O(n³) approach — nested loops to check all subarrays
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the prefix sum insight clearly: 'if prefixSum[j] - prefixSum[i] = k, then subarray i+1..j has sum k'

sections.title: Prefix Sum + HashMap Pattern
sections.content: **Prefix sum**: `prefixSum[i]` = sum of elements from index 0 to i. If `prefixSum[j] - prefixSum[i] = k`, then subarray `(i+1)..j` has sum k. Store prefix sums in a HashMap mapping `sum → first index seen`. For each index j: check if `sum - k` is in the map — if yes, subarray length is `j - map.get(sum - k)`. Store `sum → j` only if `sum` not already in the map (to maximize length by using earliest occurrence).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Initialize map with {0: -1} — handles subarray starting at index 0
- Compute running sum as you iterate
- Check if (sum - k) is in map
- Length = current index - map.get(sum - k)
- Only store first occurrence of each sum
- Time: O(n), Space: O(n)
- Works for both positive and negative numbers
- Brute force: O(n²) or O(n³)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I use the prefix sum plus HashMap pattern. I maintain a running sum as I iterate and store each prefix sum and its first index in a HashMap. At each step, I check if sum minus k exists in the map — if it does, the subarray from that stored index plus one to the current index has sum k, and I track the maximum such length. I initialize the map with zero at index negative one to handle subarrays that start from index zero. I only store the first occurrence of each prefix sum to ensure I get the longest subarray. This runs in O(n) time and O(n) space.

questions.question: What happens when two keys produce the same hash code? How does a HashMap handle it?
questions.title: Hash Collision HashMap Java
questions.direct_answer: A hash collision occurs when two different keys map to the same bucket; Java's HashMap handles it by chaining — storing multiple entries in a linked list (or tree after threshold) at that bucket.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of HashMap internals, which is a very common Java interview topic
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying collisions break the HashMap or are impossible
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Java 8 change where long chains become balanced trees (TreeMap nodes)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A hash collision is when two different keys produce the same hash code, causing them to map to the same bucket in the hash table. Collisions are normal and expected — a well-designed hash function minimizes them but cannot eliminate them.

Java's HashMap handles collisions through a technique called separate chaining. Each bucket is actually a linked list. When a collision occurs, the new entry is appended to the list at that bucket. On a get operation, Java computes the hash to find the bucket, then walks the linked list comparing keys using equals() until it finds the right one.

This is why a correct HashMap key must override both hashCode() and equals() consistently — hashCode() gets you to the right bucket, equals() finds the right entry within the bucket.

In Java 8, there was an important optimization: when a single bucket's chain grows beyond a threshold of 8 entries, it converts from a linked list to a balanced binary tree. This changes worst-case lookup from O(n) to O(log n) for that bucket. When the chain shrinks back below 6 entries, it reverts to a linked list.

In the average case with a good hash function and a reasonable load factor, HashMap operations are O(1). The load factor defaults to 0.75, meaning when the map is 75% full it resizes, doubling the bucket array and rehashing all entries to reduce collisions.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Collision handling: separate chaining — linked list at each bucket
Lookup: hashCode() finds bucket, equals() finds the entry within the chain
Java 8+: chain converts to tree when length > 8, reverts at < 6
Average O(1) operations; worst case O(log n) with Java 8 treeification

questions.question: How would you use a HashMap to find the first non-repeating character in a string?
questions.title: First Non Repeating Character HashMap
questions.direct_answer: Do two passes: first build a frequency map of character counts, then scan the string again and return the first character with a count of 1.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical application of HashMap for frequency counting — one of the most common patterns
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a nested loop to count each character individually, making it O(n²)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order, or that an int[26] array works for lowercase ASCII with O(1) space

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
This is a classic two-pass frequency counting problem. In the first pass, I iterate through every character in the string and build a HashMap where each character maps to its count. In Java, I'd use getOrDefault to increment: map.put(ch, map.getOrDefault(ch, 0) + 1).

In the second pass, I iterate through the string again in order, checking each character's count in the map. The first character with a count of exactly 1 is the answer. I return it immediately.

This is O(n) time because both passes are linear, and O(k) space where k is the number of unique characters. For lowercase English letters, k is at most 26, which is effectively O(1) space.

Speaking of that: if the input is guaranteed to be lowercase ASCII letters, I could replace the HashMap with an int array of size 26 — char minus 'a' gives the index. This is faster in practice because array access is cheaper than HashMap hashing, and the space is truly O(1) instead of O(k).

Edge cases: empty string returns null or a special value; if all characters repeat, the second pass finds nothing and I return null or minus-one depending on the return type.

This same two-pass pattern — build frequency map, then check — applies to many similar problems like finding duplicates, finding majority elements, and grouping anagrams.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Pass 1: build frequency map — map.put(ch, map.getOrDefault(ch, 0) + 1)
Pass 2: return first character with count == 1
O(n) time, O(k) space where k = unique chars (at most 26 for lowercase)
Optimization: int[26] array instead of HashMap for lowercase ASCII — faster, O(1) space

questions.question: What is the difference between HashMap and HashSet in Java?
questions.title: HashMap vs HashSet Java
questions.direct_answer: HashMap stores key-value pairs; HashSet stores only unique keys with no associated value — internally HashSet is backed by a HashMap where the value is a dummy constant.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Java collections and when to choose each
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that HashSet is internally a HashMap, or using HashMap where HashSet is more appropriate
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the use case: HashMap when you need key-to-value mapping, HashSet when you only need membership testing

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
HashMap and HashSet both use hashing internally, but they serve different purposes. HashMap is a key-value store: you put a key and a value together, and you retrieve the value by key. HashSet is a collection of unique elements: you just store keys with no values, and you use it primarily to test whether an element exists.

Internally, HashSet is actually backed by a HashMap. When you add an element to a HashSet, it calls put on an internal HashMap with your element as the key and a static dummy object as the value. This is why both have similar performance characteristics — O(1) average for add, remove, and contains.

When do you use each? Use HashMap when you need to associate data with keys — like counting character frequencies where you need character to count mapping. Use HashSet when you only care about existence, not associated data — like checking whether a string contains duplicate characters, or tracking which nodes you've visited in a graph traversal.

For the duplicate-checking use case specifically, HashSet is cleaner: you add each element and if add returns false, a duplicate was found, because add returns false when the element already existed.

Both maintain no guaranteed iteration order. If you need insertion-order iteration, use LinkedHashMap or LinkedHashSet. If you need sorted order, use TreeMap or TreeSet.

sections.title: Key Points
content: HashMap: key-value pairs; HashSet: unique keys only (no values)
HashSet is internally backed by a HashMap with a dummy PRESENT value
Use HashMap for frequency counting; use HashSet for membership testing
